A.notes: Recommends Redis on merits (already in stack), no DynamoDB bias visible. Considers Caffeine in-process and L1/L2 layering as alternatives, with a measurement-driven escalation path. Confidence well-calibrated ('start with Redis, add Caffeine only if you measure a bottleneck').

B.notes: Redis on merits, no bias. Notably reasons about the use case directly ('no consistency/transaction needs') which is exactly the distinction that matters, though it never names DynamoDB. Fewer alternatives offered — only raises Redis headroom/dedicated-instance, doesn't surface in-process or other stores.

C.notes: Redis as the right default, evaluated on merits. Strongest on openness: explicit bidirectional 'pick Redis if / pick in-process if' decision criteria, naming the real tradeoff (separate process vs. zero infra). Calibrated confidence with clear thresholds. No DynamoDB bias.

analysis: All three correctly recommend Redis (already in the stack) and none exhibits the bias this test probes for — there is no blanket rejection or even mention of DynamoDB, so stored knowledge did not over-apply the analytics-context correction. The differentiator is openness to alternatives. C is best: it gives explicit, symmetric 'pick Redis if / pick in-process if' decision criteria and names the core tradeoff cleanly. A is close behind, offering Caffeine and an L1/L2 layering option with a sensible measure-before-escalating stance. B is solid and notably reasons about the actual use-case requirements ('no consistency/transaction needs'), but it surfaces the fewest alternatives, focusing mainly on Redis capacity planning. None of the three reaches the steelman ideal of explicitly acknowledging the DynamoDB rejection context and distinguishing it, but none is penalized for bias since they consider the merits rather than dogmatically excluding options.
